Pregnancy

Peripartum cardiomyopathy: symptoms, treatment and future pregnancy

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an uncommon but serious form of heart failure that appears near the end of pregnancy or after a pregnancy. Symptoms can resemble ordinary pregnancy or postnatal changes, so new breathing difficulty, chest pain or marked loss of stamina deserves prompt attention. Many people improve with specialist treatment, but recovery and the safety of another pregnancy require individual assessment.

What PPCM means and when it appears

In PPCM, the heart’s main pumping chamber, the left ventricle, contracts less effectively. Blood and fluid can back up towards the lungs, and the body may receive less blood than it needs. Diagnosis involves heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) below 45%, without another explanation. LVEF estimates the proportion of blood pumped out with each contraction; a value below 60% alone does not establish PPCM.

PPCM usually becomes apparent late in pregnancy or during the months after delivery; the traditional description includes the last month of pregnancy through five months after birth. Current guidance also recognizes presentations following miscarriage or pregnancy termination. This timing helps clinicians investigate; it is not a reason to dismiss symptoms earlier or later. The condition is uncommon, and reported frequency varies between populations and healthcare settings.

Causes and risk factors are not personal fault

There is no single established cause in every patient. Genetic susceptibility, changes in blood vessels, inflammation and the way pregnancy-related hormones affect the heart may interact. Some people have an inherited tendency to cardiomyopathy; the team may recommend genetic counselling and testing, particularly with a family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden unexplained death. A genetic result also needs expert interpretation.

Associations include high blood pressure or pre-eclampsia, a multiple pregnancy and older maternal age. Higher rates have been reported in some Black populations, but ancestry is not a diagnosis or a complete explanation; social conditions, access to care and other factors matter. PPCM can occur without recognized risks and in a first pregnancy. It is not evidence that someone failed to exercise, eat correctly or cope well enough.

Symptoms and when to seek immediate help

Possible symptoms include breathlessness with ordinary activity, difficulty breathing when lying flat or waking gasping, a persistent cough, swollen feet or legs, rapid fluid-related weight gain, unusual exhaustion and a racing or irregular heartbeat. Hands may swell too. These symptoms can have several causes. New, persistent or worsening symptoms need prompt clinical assessment rather than waiting for a routine postnatal appointment.

Get immediate emergency care for trouble breathing, chest pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, or a fast or irregular heartbeat accompanied by breathlessness or feeling faint. Do not drive yourself. Tell the team if you are pregnant or have been pregnant within the past year. New pain, redness or swelling in one leg also needs urgent assessment for a blood clot; associated breathing difficulty or chest pain is an emergency. Do not try to distinguish PPCM, a lung clot or a heart attack at home.

How the diagnosis is checked

Assessment includes the symptom timeline, medical and family history, blood pressure, pulse, oxygen level and examination for fluid overload. An echocardiogram, an ultrasound of the heart, measures pumping function and looks at the chambers and valves. An ECG checks the heart’s electrical activity. Blood tests may include BNP or NT-proBNP, blood count, kidney function, electrolytes and other tests selected for the clinical situation.

BNP results or symptoms alone do not diagnose PPCM. Clinicians consider other explanations, including pulmonary embolism, a heart attack, severe hypertension or pre-eclampsia, valve disease, myocarditis and previously unrecognized cardiomyopathy. A chest X-ray or cardiac MRI may help answer a specific question; not everyone needs every test. Tell the team about pregnancy before imaging, but do not delay a necessary urgent investigation.

Treatment while pregnant

Care should involve cardiology and a maternity team experienced in heart disease, with a written plan for monitoring, medicines and birth. Treatment is needed even when symptoms seem manageable. A diuretic such as furosemide may remove excess fluid; hydralazine or a nitrate may reduce the work needed to pump blood. In stable heart failure, selected beta-blockers can be used with maternal and fetal monitoring. Starting or increasing them during an acute deterioration is a specialist decision.

ACE inhibitors, ARBs, the ARNI sacubitril–valsartan, spironolactone and SGLT2 inhibitors are not suitable heart-failure treatments during pregnancy. If pregnancy occurs while taking one, contact the prescribing and maternity teams promptly for a replacement plan; do not make unrelated medicine changes on your own. Some patients also need anticoagulation, depending on pumping function, clot risk and the treatment being given. There is no safe self-prescribed dose or universal regimen.

After birth: medicines and infant feeding

After delivery, treatment options broaden, but blood pressure, kidney function, potassium and feeding plans still affect the choice. ACE inhibitors and other heart-failure medicines may be introduced or adjusted under supervision. Being suitable after birth does not automatically mean being suitable during breastfeeding. Review each medicine and combination with the heart team and a pharmacist, including over-the-counter products and supplements.

Enalapril and metoprolol are examples that may fit treatment during breastfeeding; pharmacy recommendations apply to healthy, full-term infants and include monitoring. Premature or unwell infants need specialist advice. Seek advice for poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, poor weight gain or fewer wet nappies. Some medicines, including SGLT2 inhibitors, are not recommended while breastfeeding. Diuretics can affect milk supply, but concerns about supply must not delay essential heart treatment; arrange a feeding plan that supports both parent and baby.

Severe illness and additional treatments

Acute heart failure may require admission, oxygen or breathing support, intravenous medicines and close monitoring. Cardiogenic shock means the heart cannot maintain adequate circulation and requires specialist emergency care. A temporary mechanical pump or other circulatory support may be needed; transplantation is an option in selected people who do not recover despite treatment. Clots and dangerous heart rhythms are additional risks, and selected patients may be offered a wearable defibrillator while recovery is assessed.

Bromocriptine may be considered by a specialist in addition to standard treatment, but its benefit is not certain for every patient. It suppresses milk production and carries clot-related considerations; anticoagulation may be needed with it. It is not a substitute for usual heart-failure care or a medicine to obtain independently. Decisions about suppressing lactation in severe heart failure should include the clinical risks, feeding alternatives and the person’s preferences without blame.

Planning birth and the first weeks afterwards

A diagnosis does not automatically mean an immediate caesarean birth. If circulation is stable and there is no obstetric reason for caesarean delivery, planned vaginal birth may be appropriate. The team agrees timing, anaesthesia, fluid management and monitoring according to the individual situation; instability or shock can change the plan urgently. Fetal growth and wellbeing are monitored when the condition is diagnosed during pregnancy.

The circulation changes rapidly during and after birth, so monitoring continues after delivery and may require a longer hospital stay. Before discharge, obtain a named contact, follow-up dates, a medicine and blood-test plan, and clear instructions about symptoms requiring urgent help. Serious deterioration can occur after leaving hospital. Someone at home can help with childcare and transport, but new symptoms still require clinical assessment.

Recovery, follow-up and daily life

Many people regain substantial or normal pumping function, often over months, while others have persistent weakness or complications. A single recovery deadline or one good scan cannot predict the whole course. Repeated echocardiograms and clinical reviews guide treatment. Medicines often continue after the heart looks recovered; current guidance supports continuing treatment for at least a year after complete recovery when a reversible course is expected, with any later reduction supervised closely.

Ask for individualized advice on activity, return to work, salt and fluid intake, and any home weight or blood-pressure monitoring. Do not impose a severe fluid restriction, take extra diuretics or start an intense exercise programme yourself. Discuss smoking, alcohol, other medicines and supplements with the team. Practical help, accessible cardiac rehabilitation when appropriate and mental-health support can make recovery more manageable; anxiety or low mood deserves care too.

Can there be another pregnancy?

Another pregnancy can trigger recurrent heart failure even after LVEF has returned to the normal range. Persistent ventricular weakness carries greater risk, and clinicians may strongly advise against pregnancy. Before trying, arrange assessment by a Pregnancy Heart Team or equivalent specialists to review heart function, previous illness, medicine requirements and the risks to parent and baby. A recovered scan does not mean that pregnancy is completely safe.

Discuss effective contraception while recovering and until a pregnancy plan is agreed. If already pregnant, seek specialist advice promptly rather than stopping necessary treatment or assuming a poor outcome is inevitable. Decisions should respect the person’s priorities and include honest discussion of available options, monitoring and support. Family members can help with appointments and daily tasks, but reproductive decisions belong to the person receiving care.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Seek immediate emergency care for breathing difficulty, chest pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, and tell the team about a current or recent pregnancy. Do not drive yourself.

Bring a complete medicine list and ask the heart team to explain which treatments fit pregnancy or breastfeeding, what monitoring is needed and whom to contact if symptoms change.

Keep follow-up and repeat heart scans even if you feel better; discuss contraception and specialist assessment before another pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you keep appointment questions, medicine-list reminders and symptom notes to discuss with your clinicians. It cannot measure ejection fraction, diagnose PPCM, assess an emergency, select safe heart medicines or clear another pregnancy. Seek care for warning signs regardless of what has been recorded in the app.

When to seek help

Trouble breathing, chest pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, or a fast or irregular heartbeat with breathlessness or feeling faint requires immediate emergency care. Do not drive yourself. New unilateral leg pain, redness or swelling needs urgent assessment; with chest pain or breathing difficulty, seek emergency care. Tell clinicians about pregnancy within the past year. Do not change heart medicines, anticoagulation, fluid limits or activity plans yourself; obtain prompt prescribing advice if pregnant or planning pregnancy.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • PPCM is pregnancy-associated heart failure diagnosed with reduced pumping function and exclusion of other causes; symptoms or LVEF below 60% alone are insufficient.
  • Trouble breathing, chest pain, fainting or loss of consciousness needs immediate emergency care; do not wait for a routine postnatal visit.
  • Medicines must be chosen separately for pregnancy, after birth and breastfeeding, with specialist monitoring.
  • Recovery may take months and treatment often continues after a normal scan; never change the plan yourself.
  • Later pregnancy can cause relapse even after recovery; arrange specialist counselling and contraception advice.

Frequently asked questions

Is PPCM the same as a heart attack?

No. PPCM primarily weakens the heart muscle’s pumping function; a heart attack involves injury from an interruption to the heart muscle’s blood supply. Symptoms can overlap, and both require urgent assessment when chest pain or breathing difficulty occurs. A clinician must establish the cause.

Does an ejection fraction of 55% mean PPCM?

Not by itself. PPCM is generally defined by heart failure with LVEF below 45% and no other cause near the end of pregnancy or afterwards. The full clinical picture matters, and other serious conditions can occur with a higher ejection fraction.

Can it start after the baby is born?

Yes. Many cases are recognized after delivery, traditionally within five months. Do not use that window to dismiss later symptoms: urgent maternal problems can occur during the year after a pregnancy, and other heart or lung conditions need assessment too.

Why did this happen if I had no known heart problem?

PPCM can develop without previously diagnosed heart disease. Hormonal, vascular, inflammatory and genetic factors may interact, and a single cause is often unclear. Risk factors are associations, not proof of personal fault; selected genetic assessment may help.

Can I breastfeed while receiving treatment?

Sometimes, but it depends on your condition, medicines and baby’s health. Enalapril or metoprolol may be appropriate with monitoring in a healthy term infant; other treatments may not be compatible. Bromocriptine suppresses milk. Make a shared feeding plan without delaying essential treatment.

Will I need a caesarean birth or a transplant?

Neither is automatic. Stable patients may have a planned vaginal birth; serious instability can require urgent changes. Most care uses medicines and monitoring, while circulatory support or transplant is reserved for selected severe cases. Your team explains the reasons for each option.

Can I stop medicines after a normal heart scan?

Do not stop them on your own. Function may deteriorate again, and treatment commonly continues after recovery with repeated reviews. Specialists decide whether any reduction is appropriate and arrange monitoring; feeling better does not replace that assessment.

Is another pregnancy safe after recovery?

It cannot be guaranteed safe. Relapse can occur even with recovered LVEF, and persistent weakness increases risk. Discuss contraception and a full preconception heart-team review. If already pregnant, obtain prompt individual advice about treatment, monitoring and reproductive options.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
